title: The Stair
passages:
Bayo hauled the Stair rope hand over hand until the bow snapped to it, then killed the motor. The Marrow went quiet except for water sucking against the hull and the tick of cooling metal. Behind them, the Kettle's gate was shut. Ahead, the drowned towers leaned close, their windows dark and flooded, the tide already pulling them down the channel crews called the Stair.

"Wheel," Sol said.

She left the helm, stepped around the console, and lifted Nia onto the seat like she weighed nothing. Nia's boots dangled clear of the deck. Sol unfastened the paper log from its strap and laid it across Nia's knees, the page crisp with the boat rule written in ink: slates run, nobody cuts, nobody goes down alone.

"First time I've handed the wheel to anyone," Sol said. "Don't break it."

Nia looked up, ink-stained fingers tracing the line. "I can read."

"I know you can read. I'm talking about the boat."

The rope went taut at the bow, humming through the fairlead. The Marrow drifted sideways into the current. Bayo stood at the rail, counting orange splice-knots by feel, his voice coming back through the dark.

"First knot," Bayo called. "Keep her to the left of the shadow."

Nia gripped the wheel. "Left of the shadow."

"Slide three fathoms when I say mark."

Sol crossed her arms. "You ever steered before?"

Nia didn't look up from the log. "I kept Teo alive on a cold-box in Mercy General for a year. I think I can hold a wheel."

Sol snorted. "Good. Then hold it."

The tide pulled harder. The Marrow yawed, and Nia corrected, her knuckles white. Above them, a flooded tower window cracked somewhere in the dark, sharp as a gunshot.

"Next knot," Bayo said.

The rope jerked, harder this time, and the Marrow surged forward into the black. Sol opened her mouth to say something and stopped, the word gone before it reached her tongue. She let it go.

"Again," Nia said quietly.

"Again what?"

"You said something."

Sol looked at Nia's signature under the rule. "I said hold the wheel. Hold it."

The rope went taut again, and the channel narrowed.

"Mark," Bayo called, and Nia brought the wheel over.

The bow swung off the leaning tower's shadow and the current took them, and the Marrow went down the channel with the rope humming a low note through the fairlead — the oval brass eye at the bow that keeps a line from chewing through the deck.

"Slide three fathoms," Nia said. "That's eighteen feet. I did the arithmetic on the way in."

"Nobody asked for arithmetic."

"You asked if I could steer."

"Keep her left of the chimney," Bayo called. "There's a shelf on the right that'll open us up like a fish."

"Left of the chimney," Nia said, and held her.

Sol stood behind the seat with her arms crossed, watching the child work. Water sucked at the hull. Somewhere above them a window frame let go and dropped into the flood, and the sound came back off the brick twice.

"Third turn's mine to call," Sol said. "When we come round the chimney I want the engine in low, just enough to keep her off the — off the —"

Her mouth stayed open a half-beat after the rest should have come. Then it shut. Her eyes went flat and pleasant, the way a man's face goes when he pats his pockets for keys he already knows aren't there.

The Marrow swung a hand's width to starboard on her own.

Nia looked down at the log across her knees. Two pages back, in pencil gone soft with damp, in Sol's blocky hand: *STAIR. Keep left of shadow. Slide at mark. Engine low at third turn to hold off the wall. No coming about without the pilot.*

Nia read it out loud. Her voice was small and flat and it carried anyway over the water.

Sol listened to all of it with her arms still crossed.

"I wrote that," she said.

"You did. Engine low at the third turn."

"You read like a lawyer."

"I read like somebody who's still got all her hours." Nia's chin came up. "You want the wheel back, Captain, say it out loud and I'll climb down."

The tide pulled harder. It could have gone either way, and everyone on the deck knew it.

"Hold her left," Sol said. "Say it again if I go quiet."

"Every time."

"Gate's shut behind us," Nia said, eyes forward. "Lung rig's on the power barge till ten and ten's gone. So it's the rope, Bayo's hands, and mine. That's the whole way through."

"That's the whole way through," Sol said.

"Second knot!" Bayo called. "Far side of the chimney — rope's going soft, tide's making against us."

The line went slack, then came up hard enough to throw spray across the bow. Nia corrected, swore once with real fluency, and the Marrow slid past the chimney with a fathom of black water under the keel and brick close enough on both sides to touch.

"Third turn," Bayo called. "Bring her — "

The rope shivered through the fairlead.

Bayo stopped counting.
